title: AI Product Management
tagline: A 14-chapter course that takes experienced product managers to AI product management.

parts.title: How the machine thinks
parts.blurb: Accurate mental models of what an LLM is, how it is built and where its abilities stop. Everything later depends on these.

parts.title: Building blocks
parts.blurb: The four levers an AI PM actually pulls: context, evals, agents and knowledge. This is where most quality is won or lost.

parts.title: Shipping AI products
parts.blurb: Taking non-deterministic systems to production: how software gets built now, the UX of probabilistic features, reliability, unit economics and security.

parts.title: Strategy and leadership
parts.blurb: Making durable bets while the frontier moves every quarter, and reshaping the product team around it.

chapters.title: The working vocabulary
chapters.q: Can you say exactly where a model’s knowledge lives, what one request costs and how its quality is measured?

chapters.title: How LLMs are built
chapters.q: Why does a model behave the way it does, and which of its failures are structural rather than bugs?
lessons: Pretraining: next-token prediction at scale and what it actually learns
Post-training: SFT, preference tuning and RL with verifiable rewards
Reasoning models and test-time compute: buying accuracy with tokens
Why hallucination is structural, and the levers that reduce it
Tokenization quirks: counting, arithmetic, rare languages and code
Knowledge cutoffs, recency and why the model is confidently out of date
chapters.lab: Run a failure-mode probe: 30 prompts designed to break a model (counting, recency, false premises, long-tail facts). Classify every failure by cause.
chapters.out: A one-page “how our model fails” memo for one product surface.

chapters.title: Reading the frontier
chapters.q: Which model should we bet on this quarter, and how would we know if the answer changed?
lessons: The jagged frontier: superhuman and brittle in the same model
Reading benchmarks: SWE-bench, GPQA, HLE, ARC-AGI, and contamination
pass@1 versus pass^k: capability is not reliability
Model tiers and release cadence across the major labs
Running your own bake-off on your own tasks
chapters.lab: Bake off three models on 20 real tasks from your backlog. Score quality, latency and cost per task.
chapters.out: A model selection memo with a re-evaluation trigger.

chapters.title: Context engineering
chapters.q: Given a fixed model, how do you get the best possible answer through what you put in front of it?
lessons: From prompt writing to context design: what the model sees per call
System prompts, examples and structured outputs that hold up
Context rot: why more context can make answers worse
Memory, compaction and long-running sessions
Prompt caching and the economics of a stable prefix
Skills and progressive disclosure: loading context only when needed
chapters.lab: Take a failing feature and improve it with context changes alone, measured against a fixed eval.
chapters.out: A context spec: what goes in, in what order, with what budget.

chapters.title: Evals are the spec
chapters.q: How do you define “good” for a probabilistic feature precisely enough that engineering can ship against it?
lessons: Error analysis first: reading 100 real outputs before writing a metric
Golden sets, rubrics and coverage of the long tail
LLM-as-judge: when it works, how to calibrate it against humans
Offline evals, online metrics and the gap between them
Regression gates for prompt, model and tool changes
Running an eval-driven roadmap
chapters.lab: Build a 50-case eval for a live feature, run it weekly, and report the trend.
chapters.out: An eval spec that replaces the “requirements” section of your PRD.

chapters.title: Agents and tool use
chapters.q: When should a model act rather than answer, and how do you keep a long chain of actions on track?
lessons: The agent loop: model, tools, environment, stopping condition
Designing tools models can use well
MCP, A2A and skills: the emerging standard stack
Computer use and browser agents
Compounding error: why 95% per step is 36% over 20 steps
Autonomy levels, approvals and long-running background agents
chapters.lab: Build an agent with three MCP tools for a real workflow and trace every step of ten runs.
chapters.out: An agent design doc with an autonomy level and failure budget.

chapters.title: Knowledge and data
chapters.q: Should knowledge live in the prompt, in an index, behind a tool or in the weights?
lessons: Long context vs RAG vs agentic search vs fine-tuning
Embeddings, chunking, hybrid search and reranking
Freshness, permissions and provenance
Data flywheels: turning usage into quality
When fine-tuning (including RL fine-tuning) pays for itself
chapters.lab: Answer 40 questions over your own docs with long context and with RAG. Compare accuracy, latency and cost.

chapters.title: AI coding, now and next
chapters.q: Coding agents now write a large share of code. Why hasn’t software output risen to match, and what is the PM’s new job?
lessons: The landscape: IDE assistants, terminal agents, background and cloud agents
More code is not more software: review and integration become the bottleneck
Spec-driven development: the spec as the agent’s input
PMs who build: prototyping and internal tools with agents
Governance: tracing, permissions and code quality over time
Where it’s heading: longer autonomous runs, agents in CI, smaller teams
chapters.lab: Ship a working prototype with a coding agent in one day, then measure what review and hardening cost.
chapters.out: A team playbook for agent-written code: who specs, who reviews, what gets merged.

chapters.title: Designing AI experiences
chapters.q: How do you design for a system that is sometimes wrong, often slow and always a little unpredictable?
lessons: The autonomy dial: suggest, draft, act with approval, act
Calibrating trust: sources, uncertainty and showing work
Failure UX: recovery, undo and graceful refusal
Latency UX: streaming, progress and background work
Steerability and feedback that actually improves the system
chapters.lab: Redesign one existing flow at three points on the autonomy dial and test them with five users.
chapters.out: An interaction spec covering the happy path and the three most likely failures.

chapters.title: Reliability and observability
chapters.q: How do you run, debug and upgrade a system whose output changes even when your code doesn’t?
lessons: Tracing LLM and agent calls end to end
Guardrails, fallbacks and model cascades
Model upgrades: pinning, shadow runs and rollout
Drift, monitoring and incident response
SLOs for non-deterministic features
chapters.lab: Write and rehearse a model upgrade playbook using shadow traffic and your Chapter 5 eval.
chapters.out: A runbook for model changes and AI incidents.

chapters.title: Unit economics and pricing
chapters.q: What does this feature cost per user at the median and the 95th percentile, and how should we charge for it?
lessons: Cost modeling: tokens, reasoning, tools and retries
Bending the curve: routing, caching, batching and smaller models
Why AI gross margins sit below classic SaaS
Seats, usage, hybrid and outcome-based pricing
Planning for falling prices and rising usage
chapters.lab: Model cost per user at median and heavy usage for a real feature, then test three pricing models against it.
chapters.out: A pricing and margin brief for one AI feature.

chapters.title: Security, safety and governance
chapters.q: What can go wrong when a model reads untrusted content and can take actions, and who signs off?
lessons: Prompt injection and the lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted input, a way out
Permissions and sandboxing for agents
Data handling, retention and residency
Regulation: the EU AI Act and what it asks of product teams
Red teaming and launch reviews
chapters.lab: Threat-model your Chapter 6 agent and attack it with ten injection attempts.
chapters.out: A launch risk review template your security team accepts.

chapters.title: Strategy on a moving frontier
chapters.q: What will still be valuable when the next model is twice as capable and half the price?
lessons: Build for the model six months out
Where moats actually come from: workflow, distribution, data, evals
Build, buy or wrap: platform risk and model dependence
Roadmapping when capabilities arrive unannounced
Telling a credible AI story to leadership
chapters.lab: Stress-test your roadmap: which items does a 2× better model make obsolete, and which does it unlock?
chapters.out: A one-page AI strategy with explicit bets and kill criteria.

chapters.title: The AI-native product team
chapters.q: How should a product team be shaped, staffed and run when everyone can build?
lessons: Team shapes: smaller pods, PMs who build, engineers who spec
Who owns evals, context and model choice
Rituals: eval reviews, trace reviews, model upgrade days
Hiring and leveling for AI product roles
Capstone: the complete AI feature spec
chapters.lab: Capstone: take one AI feature from idea to a spec with evals, context design, agent design, economics, risks and rollout.
chapters.out: A capstone spec, reviewed by a panel from product, engineering and security.
